summary.text: 页 is the standard simplified counterpart of 頁. In modern use it writes the word for a page or sheet, through a borrowing of the traditional graph from 葉; the character’s older pictorial analysis as a head belongs to 頁, not to the visible parts of 页.

formation.text: The entry character 页 is treated as a simplified graph derived from 頁, whose head sense is analyzed as a pictograph of a kneeling person with the head emphasized. The dossier also reports an account deriving 页 from 頁’s cursive form, but does not resolve that graphic path. The pictographic analysis applies to 頁 and does not establish an internal split in modern 页.

history.text: 頁 is described in oracle-bone and bronze forms as a head-plus-body pictograph; reported forms vary in whether hair is shown. Warring States forms may distort the hair into 止, and the small-seal form omits it. The curated seal-style image is a modern vector drawing, not an ancient artifact image.

The graphic analyses of 頁 differ: one reads 卩 plus 首, while the received Shuowen text gives 𦣻 plus 几. A later textual-critical note disputes that wording, so the dossier does not settle an exact ancient component analysis. 頁 and 首 are also described as graphic variants distinguished by whether the body is drawn.

The simplified graph 页 is linked to traditional 頁 as its simplified counterpart; another account describes it as derived from cursive 頁. The dossier does not establish the specific path, and the traditional graph’s pictorial parts should not be assigned to 页.

uncertainties.text: The dossier does not establish the earliest dated use of 頁 as a common spelling for 葉 in the page or sheet sense, or a dated sequence for later uses such as “leaf.”

The proposed reuse of 頁 for 葉 is a spelling borrowing for a different word, not a demonstrated change from “head” to “page.” The historical sound match is not independently established here; modern readings and reported reconstructions do not establish the name of the depicted head or that borrowing mechanism.

Ancient-form descriptions and their interpretations are reported through database accounts; the artifact images were not independently inspected. One isolated bronze phrase is considered possibly abbreviated or erroneous.

senses.text: Modern 页 writes the page or sheet word through the traditional graph 頁, used as a common form for 葉. This is a borrowed spelling, not an established semantic development from “head.”

Oracle-bone contexts are interpreted as referring to a pig’s head and to bowing the head. This is a sourced early use of traditional 頁; it does not establish the original spoken name of the pictured head.

The dossier reports a “leaf” use alongside the page and sheet senses, but does not establish its dating or whether it is an independent single-character use rather than part of the 葉 spelling account.

developments.text: The graph 頁, used for “head,” was reused as a common spelling for the different word 葉, associated with sheets or pages. This account proposes a sound-based spelling substitution, but the historical sound match is not independently demonstrated in the dossier.

limitations.text: No verified earliest dated attestation or dated sequence of later page, sheet, and leaf uses is supplied; those glosses alone do not establish semantic chronology.
The recorded yè and xié readings and reported head-reading fanqie do not independently establish the historical sound relation behind the 葉 borrowing.

overview.text: 页 is the simplified counterpart of 頁, which was borrowed as a spelling for the word 葉, “page” or “sheet.” The older head picture belongs to 頁; its parts are not established as parts of modern 页.

takeaway.text: The page meaning comes from borrowing a spelling for 葉, not from a known change in the meaning of “head”; the historical sound match remains unverified here.

relationships.text: 页 is identified as the simplified form of 頁. A separate account associates it with cursive 頁, but the specific graphic path is unresolved.
For the traditional graph’s head sense, the two forms are described as variants of one head pictograph, differing in whether the body is drawn. This describes 頁, not internal components of modern 页.
